claims.text: Adding finely dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature and irradiation-exposed mechanical performance without compromising thermal or irradiation stability.
The proposed baseline is a MoNbTaW-type refractory high-entropy alloy having a uniform solid-solution structure.
An oxide volume fraction of approximately 1–3% is an appropriate controlled addition.
Powder metallurgy or mechanical alloying followed by hot consolidation can introduce nanoscale Y2O3 particles into the RHEA.
The intervention will produce uniformly dispersed nanoscale oxide precipitates within the alloy matrix.
The oxide particles will act as pinning centers that hinder dislocation motion.
The oxide particles will hinder grain-boundary sliding.
Hindering dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding will increase yield strength and creep resistance.
Y2O3 particles will remain thermodynamically stable at temperatures above 900°C and under irradiation.
The stability of the oxide particles will maintain the thermal and irradiation stability of the RHEA matrix.
The oxide-dispersion-strengthened RHEA will have higher yield strength than the unmodified RHEA under otherwise similar high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The oxide-dispersion-strengthened RHEA will have greater creep resistance than the unmodified RHEA under otherwise similar high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The modified RHEA will retain thermal and irradiation stability comparable to that of the unmodified RHEA.
Mechanical improvement depends on the oxide particles remaining uniformly dispersed without agglomeration.
Mechanical improvement depends on the oxide addition not causing unacceptable toughness deterioration.
Effectiveness may diminish when the oxide-particle volume fraction exceeds an optimal range.
Processing-induced undesirable phase separation may diminish the intervention's effectiveness.
